name: proposition as a first-class object
essential_semantics: A syntactic object denoting a truth-apt claim, distinguishable from a term/value; must be storable, nameable and referenced without being evaluated to a value.
canonical_example: P := 'every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes'
rationale: If claims cannot be represented separately from values, mathematics collapses into calculation and nothing can be stated, only computed.

name: truth value distinct from numeric value
essential_semantics: A Boolean-valued (or truth-value-valued) type that is not identified with 0/1 numerals and cannot be silently coerced into arithmetic.
canonical_example: (2 < 3) : Bool, and (2 < 3) + 1 is ill-typed
rationale: Conflating truth with 1/0 destroys the propositional/numeric boundary and lets nonsense such as P + 2 typecheck.

name: negation
essential_semantics: A unary connective on propositions with the standard truth condition; must scope explicitly over the whole proposition it negates.
canonical_example: not (x in S)
rationale: Negation is a minimal requirement for any logical fragment and interacts with quantifier scope, the most common source of representational error.

name: conjunction
essential_semantics: Binary connective on propositions, associative in meaning, with explicit precedence relative to disjunction and implication.
canonical_example: x > 0 and x < 1
rationale: Half of all mathematical hypotheses are conjunctions of side conditions; without it, constraints cannot be bundled.

name: disjunction
essential_semantics: Inclusive binary connective; must be distinguishable from exclusive disjunction and from case-splitting control flow.
canonical_example: x = 0 or x = 1
rationale: Disjunctive conclusions (root of a quadratic, case splits) are pervasive and are not expressible by conjunction alone.

name: material implication
essential_semantics: Directed connective between propositions whose semantics is truth-functional entailment, explicitly NOT correlation, causation, or a rewrite rule.
canonical_example: if n is even then n^2 is even
rationale: Implication is the backbone of theorem statements; conflating it with causation or with statistical association is a first-order semantic error.

name: biconditional / iff
essential_semantics: Symmetric entailment between propositions, distinct from equality of terms and from definitional equality.
canonical_example: n is even iff n mod 2 = 0
rationale: Characterisation theorems are biconditionals; representing them as equalities of terms is a type error.

name: exclusive disjunction
essential_semantics: Connective true exactly when operands differ; must be distinguishable from inclusive or.
canonical_example: exactly one of x < 0, x > 0 holds when x != 0
rationale: Derivable but frequently needed; its absence forces verbose encodings and invites mis-reading of 'or'.

name: functional completeness of the connective set
essential_semantics: The available connectives must generate every Boolean function of their arguments (e.g. {not, and} or {not, or} or NAND alone).
canonical_example: any truth table on 3 propositional variables is expressible
rationale: A classical established criterion (Post 1941); it is the correct formal notion of 'complete' at the propositional layer and is mechanically checkable.

name: predicate / propositional function
essential_semantics: A named object taking terms to propositions, with declared arity and argument sorts; applying it yields a proposition, not a value.
canonical_example: Prime(n) for n : Nat
rationale: Predicate abstraction is what lifts propositional logic to mathematics; nothing about sets, quantifiers or definitions works without it.

name: n-ary relation as an object
essential_semantics: A relation may be named, quantified over, and characterised by properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, well-founded).
canonical_example: R subset of A x A is an equivalence relation
rationale: Equivalence relations, orders and graphs are all relations; treating relations only as Boolean-valued functions loses the ability to state properties about them.

name: universal quantification
essential_semantics: Binds a variable over an explicitly given domain and asserts the body for every element; the binder, the domain, and the body must be separately recoverable from the representation.
canonical_example: for all x in R, x^2 >= 0
rationale: Nearly every mathematical theorem is universally quantified; a language that cannot bind a variable over a domain cannot state theorems at all.

name: existential quantification
essential_semantics: Binds a variable over a domain and asserts the body for at least one element; must not be silently Skolemised into a named constant unless that transformation is recorded.
canonical_example: there exists x in R with x^2 = 2
rationale: Existence claims are the other half of mathematics; their interaction with universals is where representational systems most often fail.

name: unique existence
essential_semantics: Asserts existence together with uniqueness up to the ambient equality; must be distinguishable from plain existence.
canonical_example: there is exactly one identity element in a group
rationale: Uniqueness licenses definite description ('the' inverse, 'the' minimiser); losing it makes definitions unjustified.

name: quantifier alternation and order sensitivity
essential_semantics: The representation must distinguish forall-x exists-y P(x,y) from exists-y forall-x P(x,y), and preserve that order through canonicalisation and round-trip.
canonical_example: pointwise convergence (forall eps exists N) vs uniform convergence (exists N forall eps)
rationale: The forall-exists / exists-forall distinction is the single most semantically load-bearing structure in analysis; a system that flattens it is not a mathematical representation.

name: relativised (bounded) quantification
essential_semantics: Quantification restricted by a guard, with the standard asymmetry: bounded-forall unfolds to implication, bounded-exists to conjunction.
canonical_example: for all x in R with x > 0, log(x) is defined
rationale: Guarded quantification is how side conditions attach to theorems; mis-unfolding it (using conjunction under forall) silently changes the claim.

name: quantification over functions, sets or predicates
essential_semantics: A bound variable may range over functions, subsets, or predicates rather than only over individuals.
canonical_example: for every continuous f : [0,1] -> R there exists c with f(c) = integral of f
rationale: Analysis, topology and statistics quantify over functions constantly; first-order-only systems must encode this indirectly and usually lossily.

name: binding structure and scope
essential_semantics: The representation records which occurrences of a name are bound by which binder and where the scope ends; shadowing must be resolvable.
canonical_example: in sum over i of (sum over i of a_ij) the inner i shadows the outer
rationale: Every quantifier, integral, sum, lambda and comprehension is a binder; without a binding discipline, capture bugs make the representation unsound.

name: free versus bound occurrence distinction
essential_semantics: Free variables of an expression are computable and distinguished from bound ones; a statement with unintended free variables must be rejected or flagged.
canonical_example: x^2 + y has free {x, y}; forall x. x^2 + y has free {y}
rationale: Closedness is the criterion for a well-posed statement; systems that ignore it accept open formulas as if they were theorems.

name: alpha-equivalence
essential_semantics: Renaming bound variables does not change identity; two alpha-equivalent statements must canonicalise to the same form.
canonical_example: forall x. P(x) equals forall y. P(y)
rationale: Without alpha-equivalence, structural comparison of statements is meaningless and deduplication/caching is unsound.

name: capture-avoiding substitution
essential_semantics: Replacing a free variable by a term must not capture that term's free variables under a binder.
canonical_example: substituting y for x in exists y. x != y must rename the bound y
rationale: Substitution is the engine of instantiation and rewriting; a non-capture-avoiding implementation produces false theorems.

name: equality as an assertion
essential_semantics: A symmetric relation between two terms of compatible type, asserting identity; must be distinguished from assignment, from definition, from approximation, and from 'distributed as'.
canonical_example: e^{i pi} = -1
rationale: The overloading of '=' across assertion, definition, assignment and approximation is the classic source of semantic collapse in mathematical notation.

name: definition versus assertion
essential_semantics: Introducing a new name with a defining body is a distinct speech act from asserting that two existing terms are equal; definitions are conservative and non-recursive unless declared.
canonical_example: define f(x) := x^2 + 1, versus assert f(2) = 5
rationale: If definitions and assertions are the same construct, a system cannot tell a stipulation from a claim needing proof.

name: conservativity of definitional extension
essential_semantics: Adding a definition must not permit new theorems in the original vocabulary; definitional well-formedness conditions (fresh name, no free variables, termination for recursion) are checked.
canonical_example: defining choose(n,k) := n!/(k!(n-k)!) proves nothing new about factorials
rationale: Established metatheoretic criterion; it is what makes a standard library safe to grow, and it is mechanically checkable.

name: set membership
essential_semantics: A primitive proposition relating an element to a collection, distinct from type ascription and from subset.
canonical_example: sqrt(2) in R \ Q
rationale: Domains of quantification and function domains are stated with membership; without it the guard on a bounded quantifier cannot be written.

name: set-builder / separation
essential_semantics: Forms a set from a domain and a predicate, binding the comprehension variable; the domain restriction must be explicit (separation, not naive comprehension).
canonical_example: { x in R : x^2 < 2 }
rationale: Solution sets, feasible sets and events are all comprehensions; unrestricted comprehension is inconsistent, so the domain must be part of the form.

name: subset and set equality
essential_semantics: Inclusion relation between sets with extensionality; proper versus non-proper inclusion distinguished.
canonical_example: Q is a proper subset of R
rationale: Structural comparison of domains, sigma-algebras and feasible regions all rest on inclusion.

name: union, intersection, difference, complement
essential_semantics: Boolean algebra of sets, including complement relative to an explicitly given ambient set.
canonical_example: A union (B intersect C^c)
rationale: Event algebra in probability is exactly this; unqualified complement without an ambient set is ill-defined.

name: indexed and countable set operations
essential_semantics: Union/intersection over an index set, including countably infinite index sets.
canonical_example: intersection over n in N of (0, 1/n) = empty set
rationale: Countable operations are the defining closure property of sigma-algebras and measures; finite-only set algebra cannot express measure theory.

name: power set
essential_semantics: The set of all subsets as an object that can itself be quantified over.
canonical_example: a sigma-algebra F is a subset of P(Omega)
rationale: Topologies, sigma-algebras and hypothesis spaces are subsets of a power set; without it their type cannot be stated.

name: cartesian product and tuples
essential_semantics: Product of sets/types with projection; n-ary tuples with positional typing.
canonical_example: R^2 = R x R; (x, y) with x, y : R
rationale: Joint distributions, relations, and multivariate domains all require products; encoding them as untyped lists loses arity and component types.

name: sum / disjoint union type
essential_semantics: A tagged alternative between cases, with injections and case analysis; distinguishable from ordinary set union.
canonical_example: an extended value is either a real or the symbol undefined
rationale: Piecewise and partial constructions need tagged alternatives; untagged unions lose which branch was taken.

name: indexed family of objects
essential_semantics: A map from an index set to objects, where the index is a bound variable and the family is itself an object; the index set must be explicit.
canonical_example: (X_i)_{i in I} a family of random variables
rationale: Sequences, families of random variables, matrices-as-families and parameter vectors all need indexing as a semantic construct, not as an array subscript.

name: function as a first-class object
essential_semantics: A function may be named, passed, returned, quantified over, and its domain/codomain inspected, without being applied.
canonical_example: the operator D maps f to f'
rationale: Operators, transforms, estimators and objectives all take functions as arguments; a language where functions only exist to be called cannot express them.

name: anonymous function abstraction
essential_semantics: Forms a function from a bound variable and a body, with the variable's domain recoverable.
canonical_example: x |-> x^2 on R
rationale: Integrands, objectives and transforms are anonymous functions; forcing every function to be named distorts the structure of the statement.

name: function application
essential_semantics: Applies a function to arguments with arity and domain checking; distinguishable from multiplication by juxtaposition.
canonical_example: f(x + 1) versus f * (x + 1)
rationale: Ambiguity between application and multiplication is a classic notational failure; the representation must disambiguate it structurally.

name: partiality and definedness conditions
essential_semantics: Terms may be undefined outside a domain; the representation records the definedness precondition rather than silently producing a value.
canonical_example: 1/x is defined only for x != 0
rationale: Division, logarithm, square root and matrix inverse are partial; a total-only semantics either lies or throws away the side condition.

name: typing judgement
essential_semantics: An explicit judgement that a term inhabits a type/sort, checkable and reportable, distinct from set membership as a proposition.
canonical_example: x : Real
rationale: Typing is the mechanism by which nonsense is rejected; rejection of ill-formed mathematics is the core value of a mathematical IR.

name: refinement types and controlled subtyping
essential_semantics: Types carrying a predicate (positive reals, unit interval, symmetric matrices), with a declared, non-arbitrary subtyping relation and explicit incomparability where appropriate.
canonical_example: sigma : {r : Real | r > 0}
rationale: Most mathematical side conditions are refinements; encoding them only as runtime assertions removes them from the statement's meaning.

name: types depending on values
essential_semantics: A type may mention a term (vector of length n, n x m matrix, simplex of dimension k) and typing must respect the dependency.
canonical_example: A : Matrix(m, n), x : Vector(n), Ax : Vector(m)
rationale: Shape correctness in linear algebra is a dependent-typing problem; without it, conformability is unchecked and errors surface only at runtime.

name: universes / stratification of collections
essential_semantics: A discipline distinguishing sets from proper classes or a hierarchy of universes, preventing paradoxical self-membership.
canonical_example: the collection of all groups is not a set
rationale: Rarely needed for applied mathematics, but its absence is the difference between a system that can be made consistent and one that cannot be.

name: axiom / postulate declaration
essential_semantics: A proposition accepted without proof, explicitly marked as such and attributable to a theory.
canonical_example: Axiom of Choice
rationale: Distinguishing what is assumed from what is derived is the minimal epistemic hygiene of a formal system.

name: theorem with hypotheses and conclusion
essential_semantics: A named statement with an explicit hypothesis list and a conclusion, where hypotheses are separately addressable.
canonical_example: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there is c with f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)
rationale: Theorem structure (hypotheses vs conclusion) is what allows a system to check applicability before applying a result.

name: typed context of assumptions
essential_semantics: An ordered context of variable declarations and assumptions under which a judgement holds; entering and leaving a context is explicit.
canonical_example: Gamma = {n : Nat, n > 3} entails n^2 > 9
rationale: Local assumptions inside a proof or a function body are contexts; a global-only assumption store cannot represent them without leaking.

name: generated proof obligation / side condition
essential_semantics: The system emits the conditions that must hold for a construction to be legitimate (nonzero divisor, invertibility, convergence) as first-class items.
canonical_example: using A^{-1} generates the obligation det(A) != 0
rationale: Surfacing side conditions instead of discarding them is precisely what separates a reasoning representation from a calculator.

name: proof as an inspectable object
essential_semantics: A derivation is representable, with steps, justifications and dependencies, and is checkable independently of its construction.
canonical_example: a proof of irrationality of sqrt(2) recorded as a sequence of justified steps
rationale: Only fully formal systems require this; but without any notion of derivation a system cannot claim to reason, only to state.

name: induction principle over an inductive domain
essential_semantics: Base case plus step case licensing a universally quantified conclusion, over naturals or a general well-founded order.
canonical_example: sum_{i=1..n} i = n(n+1)/2 for all n in N
rationale: Induction is the only general route to universally quantified facts about infinite discrete domains.

name: recursive / inductive definition
essential_semantics: Definition by cases referring to smaller arguments, with an explicit termination or well-foundedness justification.
rationale: Recurrences, dynamic programming and inductive data all need it; unchecked recursion makes definitions unsound.

name: well-foundedness / termination measure
essential_semantics: A relation with no infinite descending chains, usable to justify recursion and induction.
canonical_example: < on N is well-founded
rationale: It is the shared precondition of induction and recursion; stating it separately makes both checkable.

name: quotient by an equivalence relation
essential_semantics: Construction of equivalence classes as objects, with well-definedness obligations on functions defined on the quotient.
canonical_example: Z/nZ as residue classes; functions on it must respect congruence
rationale: Modular arithmetic, projective spaces and function spaces modulo a.e. equality are quotients; ignoring well-definedness produces false statements.

name: theory / signature with axioms
essential_semantics: A bundle of sorts, operation symbols and axioms that can be instantiated by a model; models and interpretations are distinguishable from the theory.
canonical_example: the theory of groups: (G, *, e, inv) with associativity, identity, inverse axioms
rationale: Abstract algebra is organised by signatures and models; without them each structure must be re-axiomatised ad hoc.

name: satisfaction relation (model models formula)
essential_semantics: The relation between a structure and a sentence it makes true, distinguishing syntactic derivability from semantic truth.
canonical_example: (Z, +) satisfies the group axioms
rationale: Needed to state independence and consistency results; optional for applied mathematics but foundational for a formal system.

name: excluded middle / constructivity marker
essential_semantics: Whether a statement or proof relies on excluded middle, double-negation elimination or choice is recorded rather than assumed.
canonical_example: a non-constructive existence proof by contradiction is flagged as such
rationale: Matters only for systems that intend to extract computation from proofs, but silently assuming classical logic is a real semantic commitment.

name: choice / selection of witnesses
essential_semantics: Selecting an element from each member of a family, with the use of choice recorded.
canonical_example: choosing a representative from each equivalence class
rationale: Included because Skolemisation and 'let x be such that' silently invoke it; a system should at least be able to name the assumption.

name: modal qualification (necessity, possibility)
essential_semantics: A statement may be qualified as necessary, possible, or holding in a specified regime, with the modality not collapsing into truth.
canonical_example: it is possible that the sequence diverges
rationale: Rarely needed in core mathematics, but modelling assumptions and applicability regimes are naturally modal and are otherwise lost to prose.

name: axiom or theorem schema with metavariables
essential_semantics: A parameterised statement standing for infinitely many instances, with metavariables distinguished from object variables.
canonical_example: the separation schema, one axiom per formula phi
rationale: Rewrite rules and generic lemmas are schemata; conflating metavariables with object variables makes instantiation unsound.
